Every instrument of the [Atlas](atlas.qmd) belongs on this page to exactly one
topic. A topic gathers instruments whose excerpts have their closest texts in the
same places, and it is named by the words that set its excerpts apart from those of
the other topics, so that a reader can see at a glance what a group of laws,
regulations, guidelines and treaties is about.

## How the topics were found

The Atlas relates every instrument to the others through a matrix. Row *i* of the
matrix says how the counted excerpts of instrument *i* spread over the other
instruments that own the text nearest to each of them, and the headings and the
transitory articles are left out of the comparison. The topics use the same matrix, in
the version that the 4B embedding model gives, which is the option the Atlas page
offers as *4B* and which was chosen because its evaluation row by row on that page is
the better of the three, for the same 2,676 unique instruments, which are 315 laws, 863 regulations, 125
guidelines and 1,373 treaties, and they group the instruments by whom they resemble,
which is what the map draws, so that a topic is a region of the map.

Four families of clustering algorithms were run, each over a fixed sweep of its one
tuning parameter, 22 configurations in all. They were density-based clustering of a
five-dimensional reduction of the rows, Ward hierarchical clustering, k-means and
Louvain community detection on the matrix read as a weighted graph. A rule fixed
beforehand chose among them. A configuration could be chosen only if it gave between
20 and 80 topics, left at most 15 % of the instruments in no topic and had no topic
larger than a quarter of the instruments, which keeps the result a map of topics and
not a split into the treaties and everything else. Among the configurations that
passed, the rule took the one that kept together the largest share of the strong
links of the Atlas, the 275 links in which an instrument names, in its title or in
its opening sentence, the instrument it develops, as the evaluation on the
[Atlas page](atlas.qmd) explains.

Only the Louvain communities passed. Ward clustering and k-means left a topic
holding from a third to three quarters of the instruments. The density-based clustering
left from a fifth to a third of the instruments in no topic when its smallest topic was
set between 5 and 20 instruments, and gave only four topics, one of them holding 94.9 %
of the instruments, when it was set to 30. The rule chose Louvain communities with a
resolution of 1.0, which gives 32 topics and leaves no instrument outside a topic. The
largest topic has 365 instruments, 13.6 % of the total, and 223 of the 275 strong links,
81.1 %, have both ends in the same topic. The silhouette of the partition is 0.030, close
to zero, which says that the instruments do not fall into well separated clouds in the
space of their rows. The topics are communities of a densely connected graph and not
compact balls, and the borders between neighbouring topics are soft.

## How a topic is named

Nobody gave a topic its name. The heading carries the three words that distinguish
the topic best, and ten are listed under it, chosen with the class-based TF-IDF of
BERTopic [@Grootendorst2022BERTopic]. All the excerpts of the instruments in a topic
are read as one document, and a term scores high when it is frequent in that document
and rare in the documents of the other topics. A term is a single word or two
consecutive words, a term had to occur in at least two instruments, and a short list
of Spanish function words such as `de`, `la` and `el` was dropped so that they would
not head every topic. Only the excerpts that the Atlas compares are read, which
leaves out headings and transitory articles.

The terms are kept as the corpus spells them, so that `artículo` and `articulo`, which
the corpus writes both ways, are two terms, and topic 7 is led by both.

## How to read a topic

The topics are listed from the largest to the smallest. A heading gives the number of
the topic and its three leading terms, the ten terms follow, and a sentence says how
many instruments of each kind the topic holds. The three most representative
instruments are those whose rows of the matrix are closest, by the cosine of the angle
between them, to the mean row of the topic. The collapsed list holds every member,
grouped as laws, regulations, guidelines and treaties, and ordered inside each group
from the closest to the mean row to the farthest, so that the first names of a group
are the ones that best stand for the topic in it. A member is written as the corpus
spells its name, followed by its abbreviation if it is a law, or by the identifier
that the Court gives it otherwise.

## An example

Topic 21 holds 43 instruments, 2 laws and 41 regulations, and its leading terms are
`sorteo`, `pronósticos` and `premios`. Its three most representative instruments are
the regulations of the Gana Gato, Tris and Pronósticos Rápidos draws of
Pronósticos para la Asistencia Pública, so that the topic is the rules of lotteries and
games. Its laws are the Federal Law of Games and Draws and the Federal Law of Public
Brokerage, and the second is a reminder that a topic is a community of instruments and
not a guarantee that every member shares its subject.
